summary: E³-Orch trains a Qwen2.5-7B orchestrator with GRPO to plan in milestones: propose an intermediate goal, build a dependency DAG of subtasks, assign each to an executor described by an anonymous capability/cost profile, and run independent subtasks in parallel. Tree-structured rollouts and separately normalized performance, cost and completeness rewards give decision-level credit. Across math, embodied and deep-research benchmarks it beats re-implemented orchestration baselines by 0.7-3.8 points with 1.16-1.59x better performance per weighted token. There are no coding tasks, and the 'cheap' and 'strong' training executors are the same 7B model.

claims.claim: E³-Orch achieves the best task performance on all seven benchmarks under both executor configurations (+0.7 to +3.8 points)
claims.evidence: Table 1: 3 runs (32 for AIME) with std ±0.2-0.6; baselines re-implemented on the same 7B orchestrator backbone and training budget by the authors. Margins are small and depend on the authors' tuning of eleven baselines.

claims.claim: The learned policy allocates work by task difficulty and executor capability-cost profiles
claims.evidence: §4.4, Fig. 6: share of model_a calls shifts by benchmark. Appendix A.7 shows model_a and model_b are both Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, differing only in context window (2048 vs 4096) and declared rank. The policy is learning a context-window and declared-cost preference, not a cheap-vs-capable model split.

claims.claim: 1.16-1.59x higher intelligence efficiency than the best baseline
claims.evidence: Fig. 4, Appendix A.13: performance per cost-weighted executor output token; orchestrator tokens and training cost are excluded; costs are declared ranks, not prices.

claims.claim: Tree-structured rollouts and decoupled reward normalization drive the gains
claims.evidence: Table 2: standard rollouts cost 3.5-4.2 points and raise tokens; removing the cost reward inflates tokens 24-82% at -0.7 to -1.9 points; scalarized reward loses 1.3-2.0 points. Ablations are averaged within family with ±0.3-1.0 std.

claims.claim: The policy transfers to executor configurations introduced only at evaluation time
claims.evidence: §4.2, Fig. 5, B.3: GPT-5-mini executors and a third Qwen2.5-14B executor; E³-Orch stays best. Only two or three executor configurations are tested.

patterns.note: Milestone-scoped planner-executor with DAG plans beats flat orchestration baselines by small margins on non-coding tasks.
Executor 'cost profiles' are routing inputs, but the training executors are one model with two context windows, so cheap-vs-expensive routing is not actually tested.
GRPO with tree rollouts and per-reward normalization improves orchestrator training over standard rollouts (Table 2).
An explicit cost reward is what keeps token use down; without it tokens rise 24-82% at similar performance.

methodology.sample: ~7,000 training instances; AIME24/25, MATH500, ALFWorld, WebShop, GAIA, HLE
methodology.baselines: Direct, ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGen, Debate, MAS-ZERO, DAAO, AgentFlow, Puppeteer, MAS-Orchestra, MasRouter — re-implemented on the same orchestrator backbone
methodology.models: Qwen2.5-7B orchestrator (3B in B.1); Qwen2.5-7B or GPT-5-mini executors; Qwen2.5-14B added in B.3
methodology.ablations: Rollout structure, branching, each reward, scalarized vs decoupled normalization, completeness reward

standards.artifacts: No code release found (uses public SandboxFusion, Math-Verify)

biases.detail: Capability-cost allocation is claimed, but the two training executors are the same 7B model; 'cost' is a declared rank.
Efficiency excludes orchestrator inference and RL training cost (tree rollouts multiply rollouts B×N×E).
All eleven baselines are re-implemented and tuned by the authors under their training budget.
AIME24/25 and MATH500 are public and likely in pretraining.
Milestones are hierarchical planning; tree rollouts and decoupled GRPO normalization are cited prior techniques.

verdict_reason: Broad benchmarks, ablations and run variance, but small margins over self-implemented baselines. The headline 'executor cost profile' behavior is learned over a pool of one model with two context windows. Self-declared work in progress.
applicability: Not a coding-harness paper and not usable by a team on hosted agents: it trains an orchestrator model. The only portable observation is that an orchestrator optimized for success alone inflates tokens, so explicit cost pressure is needed. For a Java team that is a reason to keep model choice with the host, not a design to adopt.
